topic: Bayes' Theorem: The Geometry of Changing Your Mind
target_audience: University students and data science enthusiasts

outline.topic: Bayes' Theorem: The Geometry of Changing Your Mind
outline.target_audience: University students and data science enthusiasts

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Unit Square of Probability
sections.content: Introduce the idea that the entire world of possibilities is a 1x1 square with an area of 1. Any specific event is represented as a sub-area within this square. Visualizing probability as physical space makes the upcoming 'belief shift' intuitive.
sections.example: Imagine a 1x1 square representing all possible weather outcomes. If the probability of rain is 0.2, we color a vertical strip covering 20% of the square's width.

sections.title: The Prior: Setting the Initial Map
sections.content: Define the 'Prior Probability' P(A). This is our belief before seeing new evidence. We represent this as a horizontal slice of our unit square. This establishes our baseline geometric 'territory'.
sections.example: Meet 'Robo-Guard,' a security robot. He believes there is a 10% chance a cat has entered the warehouse (P(Cat) = 0.1). Visually, we shade the bottom 10% of our square blue.

sections.title: The Evidence: Overlapping Realities
sections.content: Introduce a sensor or test (Evidence B). We map two areas: 1) The 'True Positive' area where the sensor detects the cat correctly, and 2) The 'False Positive' area where the sensor triggers even though there is no cat. These are vertical columns intersecting our horizontal slices.
sections.example: Robo-Guard has a 'Meow-Sensor.' If a cat is there, it triggers 90% of the time (Sensitivity). If no cat is there, it accidentally triggers 20% of the time (False Alarm). We draw these as vertical overlapping regions across our prior 'Cat' and 'No Cat' rows.

sections.title: The Geometric Shift: The New Universe
sections.content: The 'Update' occurs when the evidence actually happens (the sensor beeps). We discard all areas of the square where the sensor *didn't* beep. Our 'Universe' shrinks to only the sections where the sensor triggered. This is the core of Bayesian reasoning: normalising the new space.
sections.example: The sensor beeps! We zoom in, cropping the square so only the 'Beep' regions remain. The 'True Positive' area (where a cat actually exists) now occupies a new, larger proportion of this smaller, cropped rectangle.

sections.title: The Posterior: Calculating the New Ratio
sections.content: Formalize the geometry into the Bayes' Formula: P(A|B) = [Area of A ∩ B] / [Total Area of B]. Show that the probability is simply the ratio of the 'Target Success' area to the 'Total Evidence' area. This transition moves from visual intuition to the mathematical equation.
sections.example: Robo-Guard calculates: The tiny 'Cat + Beep' area divided by the 'Total Beep' area. Even though the sensor is good, the low 10% prior means the new probability of a cat is only about 33%. The geometry shows us why: the 'False Alarm' area was still quite large compared to the 'True Cat' area.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: The Unit Square of Probability
lecture_lines: Imagine a square representing all possible outcomes.
The total area is exactly one.
Specific events are sub-areas within this square.
animations: Draw a 1x1 square with a white (#FFFFFF) stroke at the center of the screen.
Fill a vertical strip from the left side, with width 0.2, in blue (#3498DB).
Add text 'P(A) = 0.2' inside the blue strip and 'P(Not A) = 0.8' in the remaining area.

storyboard.title: The Prior: Setting the Initial Map
lecture_lines: Our prior belief is the probability of a cat.
Robo-Guard estimates a ten percent chance of a cat.
We shade the bottom ten percent for this prior.
animations: Draw a 1x1 square with a white (#FFFFFF) stroke at the center.
Split the square horizontally at 10% height; fill the bottom section in blue (#3498DB).
Label the bottom section 'P(Cat) = 0.1' and the top 90% section 'P(No Cat) = 0.9' in gray (#7F8C8D).

storyboard.title: The Evidence: Overlapping Realities
lecture_lines: Now, our Meow-Sensor provides new evidence.
It triggers ninety percent of the time for cats.
It also triggers twenty percent of the time without cats.
Vertical columns represent the sensor's response.
Overlapping regions show where the sensor actually triggers.
animations: Start with the horizontally split square from Section 2.
In the bottom row (10%), color 90% of its width from the left in green (#2ECC71).
In the top row (90%), color 20% of its width from the left in red (#E74C3C).
Draw a bold white (#FFFFFF) rectangle outlining both the green and red sections.
Label the outlined area 'Sensor Beeps' and the green part 'True Positive'.

storyboard.title: The Geometric Shift: The New Universe
lecture_lines: We discard regions where the sensor remained silent.
Our universe shrinks to only the triggered areas.
animations: Fade out all parts of the square that are not green or red (the 'No Beep' areas).
Smoothly scale and move the green and red rectangles to the center of the frame.
Arrange the green and red rectangles into a single, combined vertical rectangle.
Set the height of the new rectangle to fill the square's original scale.
Label the entire new structure 'The Universe of Evidence'.

storyboard.title: The Posterior: Calculating the New Ratio
lecture_lines: Compare the cat-plus-beep area to total beep area.
The low prior keeps the final probability small.
The new probability is roughly thirty-three percent.
False alarms still occupy a significant portion of space.
This is the visual essence of Bayes' Theorem.
animations: Display the equation 'P(A|B) = Area(A ∩ B) / Area(B)' in white (#FFFFFF) at the top.
Animate a highlight on the green area, then show '0.09' in the numerator.
Highlight the total area of the new rectangle, then show '0.27' in the denominator.
Calculate and display 'P(Cat|Beep) = 33%' in the center.
Emphasize the '33%' result by circling it in gold (#F1C40F).
